(≒ fermare, arrestare, trattenere)
【General meanings】
① To stop (a person or vehicle); to bring to a halt; to call someone to a stop.
② To hold (one's breath).
③ To continue; to persist (of a state, the weather, etc.).
④ To train or urge (someone to do something).
【Musical translation examples】
“To hold back (the tempo)”; “to restrain (ritenuto)”; “to pause”; “to sustain (a note).”

In GM, it is rendered here as “slower”; in RW, as “with a pause,” among other translations. Anhalten can express active control of motion: holding back, stopping, or applying the brakes to something already in progress. In some contexts, its nuance is close to the Italian ritenuto (slower; restrained), firmly holding the tempo back at that moment. By contrast, gehalten may perhaps suggest something more like tenuto. The noun Anhalten is rendered here as “a pause”; in the GM example in Das himmlische Leben (a setting of a text from Des Knaben Wunderhorn), which reads “𝄐 bedeutet hier nur ein kurzes Anhalten auf dem Taktstrich und nicht etwa eine Fermate.” (“Here the symbol indicates only a brief pause at the barline, not a fermata”), it can be understood as controlling motion by braking or holding back something that is moving forward. One possible performance interpretation is restraint accompanied by an inner tension, like deliberately holding one's breath (Atem anhalten).
See also the entry for gehalten.

(≒ catalogo di Asow, numero Asow)
An abbreviation for the thematic catalogue of Richard Strauss's works compiled by Erich Hermann Müller von Asow (Asow-Verzeichnis), and for the catalogue numbers used in it.

The differences between TrV and AV, and why two catalogues exist: their purposes and roles

Some works by Richard Strauss (1864–1949) have opus numbers assigned during his lifetime, but many of his early and late works, studies, occasional pieces, songs, and other compositions have no opus number. Later scholars therefore compiled catalogues to organize and identify his complete output systematically. The principal examples are AV (Asow numbers) and TrV (Trenner numbers). The background to their coexistence, and their respective characteristics and roles, are as follows.

1. AV (Asow-Verzeichnis / Müller von Asow numbers)
Compiler: Erich Hermann Müller von Asow
Full title: Richard Strauss: Thematisches Verzeichnis (three volumes, issued in instalments between 1955 and 1974)
Characteristics and role: A substantial thematic catalogue (a catalogue giving the opening notes of musical themes), published after Richard Strauss's death, and a large-scale catalogue of his works.
It serves as a scholarly reference work and collection of source information, covering in great detail the thematic incipits of individual works, instrumentation, circumstances of composition, locations of autograph manuscripts, dates and performers of first performances, early printed editions, and other information. Müller von Asow died while compiling the third volume, which was supplemented and completed by Alfons Ott and Franz Trenner. The works are divided into categories, including those with and without opus numbers, and arranged chronologically within those categories. Besides works without opus numbers, the third volume includes lost works, arrangements, fragments, unrealized projects, and other material.

2. TrV (Trenner-Verzeichnis / Trenner numbers)
Compiler: Franz Trenner
Full title: Richard Strauss: Werkverzeichnis (published in 1985 / a 1993 version including thematic incipits, and a second revised edition in 1999, completed and continued by Florian Trenner)
Characteristics and role: Incorporating research and information about the works that followed the publication of Müller von Asow's catalogue, this catalogue reorganized the works as a whole in order of composition (chronological order). Its chronological arrangement (from the earliest studies of 1870 to the final works of 1949) is useful for tracing the development of Richard Strauss's creative activity and establishing and identifying dates of composition. The Richard-Strauss-Quellenverzeichnis (Richard Strauss Sources Catalogue / RSQV) takes TrV as its starting point and corrects and supplements the information about the works. TrV is also referenced in research and scholarly editions such as Richard Strauss Werke. Kritische Ausgabe (the critical edition of Richard Strauss's works), although information based on either catalogue may require correction in the light of subsequent research.

In summary:
AV: A comprehensive thematic catalogue (Thematisches Verzeichnis) for investigating thematic incipits, detailed historical and bibliographical information, and the circumstances in which works were composed.
TrV: A chronological catalogue of works (Chronologisches Werkverzeichnis) that orders and identifies the works as a whole chronologically on the basis of research available at the time of publication.

Thus, the catalogues differ in their origins and organization: an earlier, detailed thematic catalogue (AV), followed by a catalogue (TrV) that reorganized the works as a whole chronologically in light of subsequent research. However, AV also uses chronological ordering within its categories, and versions of TrV from 1993 onward also contain thematic incipits. They are consulted as complementary resources, and there are examples of both numbers appearing together in the official list of works.

② A piano damper (smorzatore), which stops a string's vibration by coming into contact with it.

【Usage notes】

Short for “Dämpfer abnehmen” or “Dämpfer absetzen.” See “Dämpfer auf.”

“Put the mute on.” In GM's usage, this is short for Dämpfer aufsetzen. Dämpfer ab means “take the mute off,” short for abnehmen or absetzen.

【Usage notes】
A mute is fitted to the bridge of a string instrument or into the bell of a brass instrument. Here, auf and ab refer to putting it on and taking it off. “Open” and “closed” in brass playing need to be read in the context of the particular technique, such as hand stopping. This is distinct from the ordinary-language pair auf (“open”) and zu (“closed”).

Emphasizes consistency over time or space: “throughout” or “without exception”, with the same state maintained across the whole.

(≒ cupo, oscuro, tetro)

③ (Of the future or an atmosphere) Ominous; threatening; sinister. Adverbially: eerily.

【Usage notes】
A rendering referring to tone colour is “with a dull tone”.
In the current GM collection, it occurs only in the first movement of Das Lied von der Erde, translated here as “gloomily”.

(≒ uguale, piano, appena, esattamente)
【General meanings】
① (Of a surface) Flat; level; smooth; even.
② (Time) Right now; just now; a moment ago.
③ (Emphatically) Precisely; exactly; just; equally (in comparisons).

(≒ ingresso, entrata)
【General meanings】
① An entrance; doorway (a place through which one enters a building, grounds, etc.).
② Arrival; receipt (of mail, documents, etc.).
③ An introduction; opening (of a story, explanation, etc.).
【Usage notes】
In specialized musical usage, Eingang can denote a short lead-in or linking passage to the return of a theme or the next section, often improvised. Einleitung is the broader term for an introduction. In RW/RS stage directions, Eingang can refer to a physical entrance.

【General meanings】
① To observe, keep or fulfill a rule, promise, deadline, etc.
② To stop; interrupt; pause.

【Musical translation examples】
"Keep the tempo or rhythm accurately"; "maintain strictly"; "observe the instruction"; "hold back the tempo"; "pause in an action or utterance".

In the current GM examples, it is translated as "slacken the tempo", rather than coming to a complete stop: holding back and easing the music’s forward movement. It should not, however, be distinguished mechanically from anhalten; whether a pause or restraint is intended depends on context.

A word expressing an indefinite number or amount. It can precede a noun or stand in place of one.
【General meanings】
① Some; a few; several; a certain amount.
② (In forms such as neuter singular einiges) Quite a lot; a considerable amount.
【Usage notes】
When referring to players, instruments, or desks, it denotes some of that group. Einige davon means “a few of them,” for example, a few of the players or instruments.

(≒ introdurre, iniziare, preparare)

③ To channel or feed (liquids, gases, etc.) into something.

Frequently found in [H]. “Begin” may be suitable, while some passages may suggest “prepare” or “lead into” the next section or tempo. The interpretation depends on the surrounding music.
[H: KM5], [H: K48], [H: K50], [H: Mat], [H: Sch], [H: Fl], [H: Welt], [RW: Oper], [GM]

② A preface, foreword, or opening passage (of a book, speech, etc.).
③ The initiation or commencement (of proceedings, measures, etc.).
【Usage notes】
In music, Einleitung denotes an introductory section or prelude to a work or movement; its length and scale depend on the work. Eingang has a specialized use for a short lead-in, for example to the return of a theme.

④ To stake (money, etc.).

The past participle of “empfinden.”

(≒ held, sustained, restrained / tenuto, sostenuto, trattenuto)

【General meanings】
① Kept, held, maintained.

【Musical translation examples】
“With the notes sustained (sostenuto)”; “sustained (tenuto)”; “restrained”; “with a restrained tone.”

GM generally renders it as “with the tempo held back,” but the translation needs to vary according to context, using expressions such as “with the notes sustained” (≒ sostenuto) or “with a restrained flow.” It may refer to sustaining the tone fully and maintaining the flow of a phrase, or to keeping the tempo or expression calm and restraining the overall flow. These meanings may overlap; where the emphasis lies depends on the placement of the marking and the surrounding context. Sustaining tone and phrasing is close to the Italian sostenuto (“supported”) or tenuto (“held”), but is not a blanket instruction to lengthen every note beyond its written value.
The comparative form gehaltener also conveys the sense of “more” or “even more.”

(≒ periodo cantabile, periodo melodico)
A compound noun formed from Gesang (“song”) + s (a linking element) + Periode (“period,” “span”).
【Musical translation examples】
“A cantabile period”; “a lyrical thematic section”; “the second theme group (especially in Bruckner's symphonies).”

This is a characteristic term used by Anton Bruckner for the “second theme group” in the sonata-form movements of his symphonies. It was not coined by Bruckner; rather, he is understood to have given substance, in keeping with his own sense of form, to a term derived from the compositional theory associated with Johann Christian Lobe. In German-language terminology, the first thematic area is called Hauptsatz or Hauptthema, and the second Seitensatz (secondary section) or Seitenthema (secondary theme). The closing area (often a third theme group in Bruckner) is called Schlusssatz (closing section) or Schlussthema (closing theme / third theme). In Bruckner, the second theme group is called Gesangsperiode (lyrical thematic section / singing period). Its character can be described as follows.

【Contrasts of character】

In Bruckner's sonata forms, the first theme (Hauptsatz) often has a “rhythmic, motivic, grand” character, contrasted with a second theme (Gesangsperiode) that is “melodic, lyrical (cantabile), and contrapuntal.” The following third theme (Schlusssatz) can display qualities such as “rhythmic energy, a powerful orchestral tutti, or a chorale-like character,” although these do not invariably occur together. This contrast suggests that the second theme is more than a merely subsidiary theme: it can be understood as a distinct, songful region (Periode).

【Structural independence】

Bruckner's “second theme” often forms an extended section (group), with several interwoven parts, rather than simply a single melody. It is therefore reasonable to describe it as a Periode (a section / a span) rather than only a Thema (theme).

The term is particularly characteristic of Bruckner and Bruckner scholarship when used for the second theme group in sonata form, but its background lies in nineteenth-century theories of form, including Lobe's.

【General meanings】

② Applied (of paint, etc.).
③ Crossed out or deleted (of letters, text, etc.).
④ Bowed (of a string instrument).
【Musical translation examples】 “sustained (with a long bow stroke)”, “drawn out (with a long bow stroke)”, “using a full bow (in Bruckner)”, “played with the bow”, “deleted”.

The word can also refer to octave notation. The prime sign (′) placed to the upper right of a note name is called a Strich (stroke); the number of these strokes indicates which octave the note belongs to. For example, “dreimal gestrichenes C” means “three-line C”.

【Use of “gestrichen” in Bruckner】
“Gestrichen” is often used to emphasise the independence of individual notes, with a strong implication of “clearly separating the individual notes (Detaché:)”. When “gestrichen” appears on its own (even though it does not follow pizzicato), it often functions as the opposite of “gebunden” (“legato”). It conveys the sense of “changing bow direction for each note (or stopping the bow) to make the separation between notes clear”.

【Use of “gezogen” in Bruckner】
“Gezogen” is often used to emphasise linear flow, frequently in contrast to “gestrichen” (which emphasises contour and accent). It is indicated when the aim is to use ample bow and emphasise a smooth, uninterrupted, “singing (cantabile)” melodic flow. The German verb “ziehen” (to draw or pull) itself has connotations of “drawing a line” and “extending something at length”. Bruckner’s symphonies are often described as “organ-like”, and the instruction “gezogen” (or “lang gezogen”) often requires string players to “sustain the tone with uniform tension, like a sustained organ tone, without allowing it to thin out when changing bow direction”. Its distinction from “legato” is that, beyond simple “legato” (connecting notes with slurs), it suggests the physical action of “maintaining constant bow speed and pressure, and playing with a full tone at length”. Incidentally, there are also passages in [B: 5] where “gestrichen” and “gezogen” are indicated at the same location.

【Use of “gestrichen” in GM】
In GM, “gestrichen” (or “wieder gestrichen”) appearing after “pizz.” or “col legno” is, in most cases, a functional reset instruction meaning “return to normal playing technique (‘arco’)”.

【Use of “gezogen” in GM】
Use in combinations: “gezogen” never appears on its own, but is always combined with “lang” (long) or “breit” (broad), as in “lang gezogen” (drawn out at length), to specify note duration or the length of phrasing.

For these reasons, it is best to avoid confusing these terms in Bruckner with “arco” in the GM sense. Put simply, in GM they would concern “How to play”, whereas in Bruckner they would concern “How it sounds”.

(≒ steward, majordomo, butler / maggiordomo, intendente)

【General meanings】
(In older usage) A steward, butler, or household administrator who manages the domestic affairs of a large residence or court and supervises its servants.

The following is a guide to servants, attendants, and domestic workers in Richard Strauss’s Der Rosenkavalier, Op. 59. Even the same terms—Diener, Lakai, and Livree—can have substantially different functions depending on whose household they belong to. It is therefore useful to distinguish the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, Baron Ochs’s entourage, and the inn staff. Octavian’s own attendants, who appear in Act II, must also be distinguished. Since differentiating every term in translation would become extremely cumbersome, some are grouped together on the search page.

【Qualification concerning rank】
The ranks given below and the hierarchy at the end are provisional classifications from the original draft; they have not been verified as a uniform historical hierarchy of posts. Duties, relationships with the employer, household affiliation, and assessments of characters on stage must be distinguished. In particular, the same Leopold is called Kammerdiener, junger Kammerlakai, Leibkammerdiener, Leiblakai, Lakai, and other names in this work. Differences in terminology therefore cannot simply be taken to indicate separate characters or differences in social rank.

●Almosenier
A post responsible for administering alms, or a disreputable former cleric. Originally, this was the title of a cleric responsible for charitable work at a court or in the residence of a great noble. When Baron Ochs uses this word, its archaic, grandiose sound itself comically conveys his character as an anachronistic provincial nobleman.
【Rendering used】Almoner
【Rank: low】One of Baron Ochs’s personal followers. Despite his pompous title, he is in fact a dubious former cleric whose social standing is incomparably lower than that of the regular servants in the Marschallin’s household.

●Bediente
“Household servant,” with a somewhat official, impersonal tone. More formal than Diener, it strongly suggests a member of the “staff” employed by a household or master. The emphasis is on the staff as a group rather than on individual personalities.
【Renderings used】Household servant, household servants
【Rank: middle to lower】A general term for male servants. It refers primarily to ordinary workers who support the running of the residence, rather than to senior posts such as steward or valet. It is approximately equivalent in rank to Diener (servant), but Bediente has a somewhat more institutional or organizational tone.

●Diener
The broadest and most basic term for “one who serves.” It is not restricted to any particular duty, but focuses on the act of serving a master. It is close to the nuance of personal service conveyed by the Japanese word servant (“servant”).
【Renderings used】Servant, servants
【Rank: middle to lower】The basic rank of male servants: an ordinary servant without a special job title. It is approximately equivalent in rank to Bediente (household servant), but Diener more strongly suggests an individual serving another person. In Der Rosenkavalier, however, an unqualified Diener does not always refer to the same household affiliation: depending on the context, he may belong to the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, or Baron Ochs’s entourage.

●Dienerschaft
The entire body or organization of servants. A collective noun referring to an organized staff headed by a steward. The standing of a residence is reflected in the quality and size of its Dienerschaft.
【Renderings originally preferred】Servants; depending on the context, “attendants” or “the household staff”
【Rank: the entire structure】The basic rendering is “servants,” in keeping with Diener. Depending on the scene, however, it may be translated flexibly as “the household staff” or “attendants.” When used of Baron Ochs’s entourage, it often refers to his uncouth followers rather than to a refined household organization.

●Duenna
A supervisor or guardian of a young noblewoman. A specialized post originating in the Spanish court, often functioning as a nagging, conservative supervisor of female attendants.
【Rendering originally preferred】Chaperone
【Designation used】Duenna (Marianne)
【Rank: upper-middle】Sophie’s personal chaperone. She ranks above ordinary maids and has authority to supervise the young lady’s conduct, manners, and formal interactions. In Der Rosenkavalier, Jungfer Marianne Leitmetzerin can be treated as the character who performs this function.

●Faninals Bediente / Diener / Livree / Lakaien
Collective designations for the household servants, servants, footmen, and liveried footmen serving Faninal’s household. The libretto varies its terminology according to the scene, using such expressions as Faninalsche Bediente, Faninalsche Diener, Faninalsche Livree, and Faninalsche Lakaien. All can be classified as the body of servants belonging to Faninal’s residence.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Bediente: household servants
Diener: servants
Livree: liveried footmen
Lakaien: footmen
【Rendering used】Faninal’s household servants
【Rank: middle to lower / household organization】In Act II, during the ceremonial presentation of the rose, they open and close doors, arrange chairs, serve wine and sweets, and receive visitors, visually expressing the standing of the household established by the upstart nobleman Faninal. At the same time, they become caught up in the uncouth behavior of Baron Ochs’s attendants, highlighting the breakdown of order within the house. In Act III, they assist Faninal and Sophie, who have hurried to the inn, and tend to Faninal when he is on the verge of fainting. They thus function as a group that sustains the stage portrayal of both the Faninal household’s dignity and its confusion. Although there are fine distinctions in meaning, it should be acceptable to group them under “Faninal’s household servants.”
【Note】Haushofmeister bei Faninal (the steward of Faninal’s household) is best considered separately as the managerial official who supervises this group.

●Hausknecht
A menial worker employed at an inn, a merchant’s establishment, or similar premises. Responsible for physical labor and of the lowest rank. He belongs to a different category from the servants in an aristocratic residence.
【Rendering used】Domestic laborer
【Rank: lowest / inn staff】A coarse menial worker employed behind the scenes at the inn. He appears in Act III and reinforces the inn’s practical, everyday atmosphere. He belongs to a different system from the hierarchy of servants in an aristocratic residence.

●Haushofmeister
A steward or head butler who oversees an entire residence belonging to a great noble or wealthy household. He heads the organization of servants and supervises ceremonial arrangements, finances, household operations, and the reception of visitors.
【Rendering originally preferred】Head butler
【Rendering used】Steward
【Rank: highest managerial post】The highest rank in the hierarchy of male servants in a residence. An important official who directs the Diener, Lakai, Bediente, and others and embodies the household’s standing. Both the steward of the Marschallin’s household and the steward of Faninal’s household make their employers’ social status visible on stage.

●Kammerdiener
A personal attendant serving in his master’s private rooms. Responsible for dressing him, looking after his personal belongings, and carrying out private errands; his master’s trust is essential.
【Rendering used】Valet
【Rank: high】A specialized post ranking above ordinary footmen. He is experienced and holds a high position because of his loyalty to his master and his permission to enter the master’s private space. Baron Ochs’s Kammerdiener, however, is portrayed as an uncouth, slovenly attendant, in contrast to the refinement originally associated with this title.

●Kammerlakai
A lower-ranking footman attached to the private rooms. He assists the valet and performs miscellaneous duties around the private apartments.
【Rendering originally preferred】Chamber footman
【Rank: middle】Below a Kammerdiener, but more closely connected to the private rooms than an ordinary Lakai. In Der Rosenkavalier, the term sometimes appears as a designation for Baron Ochs’s young close attendant Leopold and overlaps functionally with Leiblakai. For practical classification, it is therefore useful to group it with Leiblakai / junger Kammerlakai / Lakai des Barons.

●Kellner
A waiter employed at a commercial establishment, particularly an inn or restaurant. Not a servant in an aristocratic residence.
【Rendering used】Waiters
【Rank: external】Employees outside the hierarchical structure of aristocratic society. In the inn scene in Act III, they attend to the table, lighting, food, wine, and entrances and exits, arranging Baron Ochs’s secret rendezvous with Mariandel as an ordinary meal. Near the end, they join the Wirt (innkeeper), Musikanten (musicians), Hausknecht (domestic laborer), and others in crowding around the Baron to demand payment of bills and service charges, reducing aristocratic dignity to the obligation to pay in a commercial setting.

●kleiner Neger
A Black boy attendant responsible for carrying the train of a garment and performing duties like those of a personal servant. A decorative presence used to display status. The term is now discriminatory and requires care.
【Rendering used】Black boy
【Rank: special (lower)】His role is to carry the Marschallin’s train. Although a type of footman, he is less part of the ordinary hierarchy of servants than a decorative presence employed for aristocratic display, exoticism, and the demonstration of status.

●Lakaien / Bediente der Feldmarschallin
The group of footmen serving in the Marschallin’s residence. In Act I, they try to prevent Baron Ochs from forcing his way in and guard the boundary between the bedroom and the antechamber. During the morning reception, they also open and close doors, move furniture, organize visitors, and coordinate the movements of the Friseur, Sänger, and others.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Lakaien: footmen
Bediente: household servants
【Rendering used】The footmen of the Marschallin’s household
【Rank: middle to lower / servants in a great aristocratic residence】They belong to a separate organization from Faninal’s household servants and Baron Ochs’s attendants. They show that the Marschallin’s residence, although the setting is her private bedroom, is also a highly organized aristocratic space.

●Lakai
A lower-ranking footman in a residence. Responsible for miscellaneous duties such as opening and closing doors, showing visitors in, and running errands; he is often also stationed for ceremonial purposes or visual effect.
【Rendering used】Footman
【Rank: lower】Equivalent to, or slightly below, Bediente and Diener. He ranks considerably below a valet. He wears livery to display his master’s household standing but has no personal authority or managerial position. In Der Rosenkavalier, he may belong to the Marschallin’s household, Faninal’s household, or Baron Ochs’s entourage. It is therefore clearer to include his affiliation in the translation rather than simply calling him a “footman.”

●Leibjäger
A huntsman and bodyguard attached exclusively to his master. A rugged figure accompanying a provincial nobleman.
【Rendering used】Bodyguard-huntsman
【Rank: special (low)】Rather than a regular household servant, he is one of the personal followers whom Baron Ochs has brought from the countryside. He is portrayed as embodying ruggedness, intimidation, and the coarseness of the provincial nobility rather than manners or refinement.

●Leibkammerdiener
A personal valet who serves his master in close attendance. Responsible for the most confidential duties in the private rooms.
【Rendering used】Personal valet
【Rank: very high】Even closer to his master than a Kammerdiener, and equivalent to the highest rank among footmen. In Baron Ochs’s case, however, he may be portrayed as an uncouth member of the Baron’s personal entourage rather than as a senior valet possessing formal courtly refinement.

●Leiblakai
A footman in his master’s personal service. Not as high-ranking as a Kammerdiener, but close to his master.
【Rendering used】Personal footman
【Rank: special (low)】He has a special relationship with his master but is of low social standing. In Baron Ochs’s case, he is implied to be an illegitimate son and is portrayed as poorly trained and unrefined. Formally, he is a footman serving as a close attendant; in practice, he is an uncouth follower of a provincial nobleman.

●Leiblakai / junger Kammerlakai / Lakai des Barons
The young personal attendant closest to Baron Ochs. In the libretto, he can be classified as the character functioning as Leiblakai, junger Kammerlakai, and, in some scenes, Lakai des Barons.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Leiblakai: personal footman
junger Kammerlakai: young chamber footman
Lakai des Barons: the Baron’s footman
【Rendering used】Personal footman
【Rank: special (low)】He carries the case for the silver rose, accompanies the Baron to his secret rendezvous at the inn, and tries to clear a path for the Baron’s departure near the end. He is also implied to be the Baron’s illegitimate son and visually conveys the private, disorderly domestic arrangements of the Lerchenau household.

●Leute / Livree / Diener / Dienerschaft des Barons
Collective designations for the personal followers and body of liveried footmen whom Baron Ochs has brought from the countryside. Leute emphasizes their function as “the Baron’s people or followers”; Livree emphasizes their appearance and display of status as “a body of footmen in livery”; Diener / Dienerschaft emphasizes the organization of servants attending the Baron.
【Renderings originally preferred】
Leute des Barons: Baron Ochs’s followers
Livree des Barons: Baron Ochs’s body of liveried footmen
Diener des Barons: Baron Ochs’s servants
Dienerschaft des Barons: Baron Ochs’s organization of servants
【Rendering used】Baron Ochs’s attendants
【Rank: low / uncouth】They include the Almosenier, Kammerdiener / Leibkammerdiener, Leibjäger, Leopold / Leiblakai, and others. In contrast to the refined servant organizations of Vienna, they are portrayed as slovenly and uncouth in their behavior. In Act II, they behave in an intimidating and violent manner toward Sophie and Faninal’s household servants, collectively amplifying Baron Ochs’s vulgar character. In Act III, they again try to preserve the Baron’s dignity, but become caught up with the inn staff and the unfolding trap, visually heightening the collapse of his authority.

●Livree
Livery, or the body of footmen wearing it. A term symbolizing the authority of a household.
【Renderings originally preferred】Livery, liveried footmen
【Rank: symbolic】The quality of the tailoring symbolizes the household’s standing. When the term appears on its own, it may be translated as “livery” or “liveried footmen.” For Baron Ochs’s entourage, however, it is easier to classify it together with Leute / Livree / Diener / Dienerschaft des Barons (Baron Ochs’s attendants), and for Faninal’s household, with Faninals Bediente / Diener / Livree / Lakaien (Faninal’s household servants).

●Lümmel
An uncouth young man or lout. An insult, not a particular job title.
【Rendering used】Lout
【Rank: lowest stratum / outside the hierarchy】Not a formal rank among servants. The word indicates the coarseness, lack of manners, and violence of Baron Ochs’s followers and should be treated as an assessment of character or an insult rather than as a social rank.

●Magd
An ordinary female servant. Responsible for domestic work such as cleaning, laundry, and kitchen duties.
【Renderings used】Maid, maids
【Rank: lower】The basic rank of female servants. Below a Zofe. In Act II, the maids are chased by Baron Ochs’s attendants, revealing the coarseness of his party and the breakdown of order in Faninal’s residence.

●Zofe
A lady’s maid who attends to the personal needs of a noblewoman. A highly trusted figure.
【Rendering used】Lady’s maid
【Rank: high (among female servants)】Considerably higher-ranking than an ordinary maid. She is close to her mistress’s private life and may become a confidante. In Rosenkavalier, however, this is the designation used when Octavian disguises himself as Mariandel.

【Classification by rank: for reference only】
The following is not a verified hierarchy. In particular, note that alternative designations for the same person are sometimes placed at different levels.

【Very high (attached exclusively to the master personally)】

【Upper-middle (supervisory role)】

【Middle (lower-ranking posts connected with the private rooms)】

【Middle to lower (ordinary male servants)】

Diener (servant)
Lakai (footman)
Lakaien / Bediente der Feldmarschallin (the footmen of the Marschallin’s household / more specifically, “footmen,” “household servants”)
Faninals Bediente / Diener / Livree / Lakaien (Faninal’s household servants / more specifically, “household servants,” “servants,” “liveried footmen,” “footmen”)

【Lower (ordinary female servants)】

【Lower (followers of provincial nobles and similar attendants)】
Almosenier (almoner)
Leute / Livree / Diener / Dienerschaft des Barons (Baron Ochs’s attendants / more specifically, “followers,” “body of liveried footmen,” “servants,” “organization of servants”)

【Special (outside the residence, or with a particular background)】

Leibjäger (bodyguard-huntsman)

(≒ domestico, facchino)
【General meanings】
① A male domestic servant or general odd-job worker.
② In older usage, a porter or luggage carrier at an inn or similar establishment.

For the servants in Der Rosenkavalier, see “Haushofmeister”.

(≒ veemente, intenso)
【General meanings】
① Violent, vehement, or intense.
② Fervent, hot-tempered, or passionate in temperament or emotion.
③ Severe, as of an illness.
【Musical translation examples】
“vehemently”, “violently”, “with intense emotion”.

It seems to have both positive and negative uses comparable to the Japanese slang word “yabai”: “Das Konzert war heftig!” (“That concert was intense!”).

(≒ santo)
An inflected form of Heilige(r), the noun formed from heilig; it may, for example, be plural.
【General meanings】
① A saint or holy person in Christianity or another religion.
② Figuratively, a person who is the object of veneration.

(≒ segreto, misterioso)
【General meanings】
① Secret, confidential, or concealed.
② Surreptitious, furtive, or discreet in action.
【Usage notes】
When describing the expression of a voice or musical sound, a contextual rendering is “with a secretive sound”.

(≒ sereno, allegro)
【General meanings】
① Cheerful, bright, or serene, as of a mood, atmosphere, or sky.
② Optimistic or cheerful in character or outlook.
③ Clear or fair, as of the weather.
【Usage notes】
For the expressive character of the tone, “with a bright tone” is a possible rendering. In GM, it is translated as “cheerfully”.

(≒ fuori, da dentro)

【General meanings】
① Out from inside to outside, towards the speaker or another point of reference.
② Figuratively, into the open or becoming apparent.
③ As a separable verb prefix, it can add the sense of extracting something, finding it out, or distinguishing it: for example, heraushören, to distinguish by ear, and herausfinden, to find out.

(≒ proposta editoriale)
A compound noun formed from Herausgeber (critical editor or editor) and Vorschlag (suggestion).
【General meanings】
An editor’s suggestion or proposal.
【Usage notes】

A number assigned by the Swiss musicologist Willy Hess in his Verzeichnis der nicht in der Gesamtausgabe veröffentlichten Werke Ludwig van Beethovens, published in 1957.

The Hess catalogue was not compiled simply to classify works without opus numbers. It catalogues works and materials omitted from the old Beethoven complete edition published by Breitkopf & Härtel in the nineteenth century. It therefore includes not only independent, completed works but also first versions, alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, and composition exercises. Hess numbers can also be assigned to alternative versions or arrangements of works that have opus or WoO numbers, so the Hess, Op., and WoO systems are not mutually exclusive.

However, not all of the vast quantity of sketches left by Ludwig van Beethoven have Hess numbers. The Hess catalogue includes works and materials omitted from the old complete edition that Willy Hess considered necessary to identify and classify separately. It is therefore not a comprehensive catalogue of Beethoven’s sketches.

Whereas WoO numbers are used to classify works without opus numbers, Hess numbers are supplementary catalogue numbers for works and creative materials omitted from the old complete edition. The two catalogues have different inclusion criteria, and neither simply contains the other. The Hess catalogue includes completed works as well as alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, and composition exercises; WoO also exceptionally includes unfinished works.

In 2014, a revised catalogue, Ludwig van Beethoven: Thematisch-bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, by Kurt Dorfmüller, Norbert Gertsch, Julia Ronge, and collaborators, was published. It retains the established Op. and WoO numbers and assigns Unv (Unvollendete Werke) 1–23 to a selection of unfinished works not included in the previous catalogue. Hess numbers are not its principal classification numbers, but they are given alongside the relevant entries or sources, and a concordance is provided.

Hess numbers may thus be understood as historical supplementary numbers assigned by Willy Hess to identify completed works, alternative versions, arrangements and reworkings, unfinished works, fragments, sketches, composition exercises, and similar materials omitted from the old Beethoven complete edition. They continue to be used to cross-reference older literature, scores, recordings, and research.

See also “WoO”.

An abbreviation for the catalogue of Joseph Haydn's works (Hoboken-Verzeichnis) compiled by the Dutch musicologist Anthony van Hoboken. Works are classified by genre and identified by a Roman-numeral group number followed by a number within that group. For example, Symphony No. 100 in G major is Hob. I:100. Groups I–XXXI are listed below; there is also a group XXXII for pasticcios.

Hob. I: Symphonies (Symphonien)
Hob. II: Divertimenti in four or more parts (Divertimenti in 4 und mehr Stimmen)
Hob. III: String quartets (Streichquartette)
Hob. IV: Divertimenti in three parts (Divertimenti in 3 Stimmen)
Hob. V: String trios (Streichtrios)
Hob. VI: Various duos (Verschiedene Duos)
Hob. VII: Concertos for various instruments (Konzerte für verschiedene Instrumente)
Hob. VIII: Marches (Märsche)
Hob. IX: Dances (Tänze)
Hob. X: Various ensembles or divertimenti involving baryton (Werke mit Baryton / Divertimenti mit Baryton)
Hob. XI: Baryton trios (Barytontrios)
Hob. XII: Duos involving baryton, including those with a bass part (Duos mit Baryton, mit und ohne Bass)
Hob. XIII: Baryton concertos (Barytonkonzerte)
Hob. XIV: Divertimenti with piano (Divertimenti mit Klavier)
Hob. XV: Trios for violin (or flute), cello, and piano (Trios für Klavier, Violine (oder Flöte) und Violoncello)
Hob. XVI: Piano sonatas (Klaviersonaten)
Hob. XVII: Short piano pieces (Klavierstücke)
Hob. XVIII: Keyboard concertos (Klavierkonzerte)
Hob. XIX: Pieces for mechanical musical clocks (Stücke für Spieluhren)
Hob. XX: The Seven Last Words of Our Saviour on the Cross (Die sieben letzten Worte unseres Erlösers am Kreuze)
Hob. XXI: Oratorios (Oratorien)
Hob. XXII: Masses (Messen)
Hob. XXIII: Other sacred works (Kirchenwerke)
Hob. XXIV: Cantatas, choruses, and arias with orchestral accompaniment (Kantaten, Chöre und Arien mit Orchester)
Hob. XXV: Songs for several voices, including duets, trios, and quartets (Mehrstimmige Gesänge)
Hob. XXVI: Songs with piano accompaniment, and cantatas and choruses accompanied by a single instrument (Lieder mit Klavierbegleitung; Kantaten und Chöre mit Begleitung eines Instruments)
Hob. XXVII: Canons (Kanons)
Hob. XXVIII: Operas (Opern)
Hob. XXIX: Marionette operas and Singspiele (Marionetten-Opern und Singspiele)
Hob. XXX: Incidental music (Schauspielmusiken)
Hob. XXXI: Arrangements of Scottish and Welsh folk songs, and other arrangements (Bearbeitungen schottischer und walisischer Volkslieder und andere Bearbeitungen)

A Black pageboy.

“Neger” was formerly used in Europe to refer to Black people, but is now regarded as a discriminatory term. When it appears in historical librettos or scores, it needs to be understood as an expression reflecting the society and racial attitudes of its time.

A related musical work is Claude Debussy’s Golliwogg’s Cake-walk. It is the sixth piece in the suite Children’s Corner, and the Golliwogg in its title refers to a rag doll caricaturing a Black person. The figure became widely known through a picture book published in 1895 and illustrated by Florence Kate Upton, and was also popular as a children’s toy. Its features, including its black face, large eyes and exaggerated lips, are connected with the imagery of contemporary minstrel shows, in which performers blackened their faces to portray Black people, and embody racial stereotypes.

The cakewalk is a dance that developed among enslaved Black people in America. One aspect of it involved imitating and satirizing the affected gestures and dances of the white upper classes. Its name derives from the practice of awarding a cake to the winner of a dance competition. It later spread through Europe and America as a form of stage entertainment and was also incorporated into Debussy’s music. In Golliwogg’s Cake-walk, both the dance and the doll bring together the reception of Black culture and representations of Black people at the time.

Debussy also composed a separate short piano piece using cakewalk rhythms, Le petit nègre (the little Black person).

In the Glockenspiel part of the first movement of GM’s Symphony No. 7, “mit Klöppeln” is translated here as “with mallets”, although from a modern perspective it is perfectly normal to play a glockenspiel with mallets. However, keyboard glockenspiels (Tastenglockenspiel) were also in use in Mahler’s time, and a keyboard glockenspiel may well have been assumed in Symphony No. 7. For example, the No. 20 aria in Mozart’s Die Zauberflöte (Bärenreiter, p. 258) is marked “Strumento d’acciaio (Glockenspiel)” (“instrument of steel”); its many chords and rapid passages also provide grounds for interpreting the writing as conceived for a keyboard glockenspiel. On that reading, an instruction to play with mallets rather than the keyboard makes sense.

Lady Macbeth. O, eile! Eile her! damit ich meinen Geist in deinen giesse, durch meine tapfere Zunge diese Zweifel und Furchtgespenster aus dem Felde schlage, die dich wegschrecken von dem goldnen Reif, womit das Glück dich gern bekrönen möchte.

The German heading comes from Schiller’s adaptation (Act 1, Scene 9). The corresponding original passage in Shakespeare’s Macbeth, Act 1, Scene 5, reads as follows.

Lady Macbeth:
Hie thee hither,
That I may pour my spirits in thine ear,
And chastise with the valour of my tongue
All that impedes thee from the golden round,
Which fate and metaphysical aid doth seem
To have thee crown’d withal.

【Translation of the German quotation】
O, hurry! Come quickly!
Then I could pour my resolve into you,
and with the force of these courageous words
drive away all the doubts and spectres of fear
that keep you from the golden crown (kingship).
For fortune (fate) would gladly crown you with that crown.

The scene can be interpreted as follows. Having read Macbeth’s letter describing the witches’ prophecy, Lady Macbeth sees that her husband is “too kind to resolve to become king”. She decides to take on the task of pouring that resolve into him and driving out his hesitation through words. Here, “Geist” (“spirit”) means courage, boldness, and the ability to make ruthless decisions, while “tapfere Zunge” (“valiant tongue”) shows her awareness of the power of manipulative language as a weapon. “Goldner Reif” (“golden circlet”) is an indirect expression for the crown, while “Glück” (“fortune” or “luck”) can also be read as a perilous turn of phrase that presents the temptation to sin as though it were fate’s blessing.

(≒ suono della natura)
【General meanings】 ① A sound of nature (birdsong, wind, a murmuring stream, etc.). ② An inarticulate cry or instinctive vocal sound.

GM uses the term in Symphonies Nos. 1 and 3. It means “a sound of nature (the resonance of the natural world)”. In Symphony No. 1, “Wie ein Naturlaut” (translated here as “like a sound of nature”) can be understood as going beyond mere “nature painting”, with a strong suggestion of “something other than an artificially ordered musical tone”. It may be interpreted as a sound originating outside the music (in nature), as though it had already been sounding before the music began: a resonance suggestive of “ambient sound”. In Symphony No. 3, when the direction for the oboe is combined with “hinaufziehen”, translated as “upward portamento”, the intended effect is probably a mingling of uncontrived natural sound rather than “ambient sound”.

【General meanings】
① Resonance; reverberation; the sounding or echoing of sound.
② Resonance (in physics or electricity).
③ (Figuratively) Sympathy; response; public reaction.

Mahler uses this instruction for the harp. There it is rendered as “soundboard (play very close to it)”. The likely aim is a harder, more metallic sound with a quicker attack. “Resonanztisch” likewise means “soundboard”: “Tisch” refers to a “table” or “flat surface”.

(≒ dolce, mite)
【General meanings】

② Soft, or faint depending on context, of sound, tone quality, or light; quiet, of sound.
③ Gentle, of a slope, etc.
【Usage notes】
For the GM examples, this glossary renders sanft as gently (“gently”). It renders mäßig as a tempo indication as gently（at a moderate tempo） (“calmly, at a moderate tempo”). (≒ padiglione)
【General meanings】
① The bell of a wind instrument.
② A sound-reinforcing component, as in older acoustic devices.

A general term for the end of a woodwind or brass instrument and for the resonator of certain organ reed pipes. In wind-instrument contexts, it is broadly synonymous with Schalltrichter and Schallstück. On the horn, it denotes the part into which the right hand is inserted for stopped playing or tone modification.

(≒ padiglione, imbuto sonoro)
Synonymous with Schallbecher when referring to the bell of a wind instrument.
【General meanings】
① The bell of a wind instrument.
② A conical part that amplifies sound; a megaphone.

“Schall” means “sound” or “resonance”.
“Bells up” can be expressed in several ways, including mit aufgehobenem Schalltrichter, Schalltr. auf, and Schalltrichter in die Höhe. Here, “aufgehoben” means “raised”, and “in die Höhe” means “upward” or “up high”.
The bell is also called Schallbecher. No occurrence of Schallbecher has been found in the GM material under investigation, although the word does occur in other score material. In the [RW: Oper] material examined here, Schalltrichter occurs only in Tristan und Isolde.

(≒ trascinare, levigare)
“schlifen” is probably a misprint.
【General meanings】
① To sharpen, polish, or grind (a blade, etc.).
② To drag along (the ground, etc.); to walk dragging one's feet.
③ (In the expression “schleifen lassen”) To neglect something; to let it slide.
④ To demolish or raze (fortifications, etc.).
【Musical translation examples】
“slur the notes together”, “slide smoothly”, “connect the notes with a dragging or sliding motion”.

In [RS: Held] (Ein Heldenleben), it denotes portamento.

(≒ trascinare)
【General meanings】
① To drag, pull, or haul (something heavy).
② To trail along the ground (of clothing, etc.).
③ To drag on (of time, etc.).
【Musical translation examples】
“drag (the tempo)”, “slow down”, “let the rhythm become sluggish”, “do not drag the tempo (for nicht schleppen)”.

In GM, the Japanese rendering of “schleppend” is “引きずるように” (“dragging”), and that of “nicht schleppend” is “引きずらないで” (“without dragging”). Still, “緩慢に” (“sluggishly”) may be preferable for the former, and “緩慢にならないで” (“without becoming sluggish”), “遅くならないで” (“without slowing down”), or “間延びしないで” (“without letting the music drag out”) for the latter.

(≒ semplice, schietto)
【General meanings】
① Simple; plain; unadorned.
② Unpretentious; sincere; natural.
③ (Literary, of hair) Smooth; straight.
【Musical translation examples】
“simply”, “without ornament”, “straightforwardly”, “unaffectedly”.

In GM, the Japanese rendering is “素朴に” (“simply”).

(≒ languido, sospirando)
Present participle of “schmachten”.
【General meanings】
① Pining; yearning; suffering (from love, hunger, etc.).
② Evoking pity; feeble; faint (of a voice or expression).
【Musical translation examples】
“with longing”, “imploringly”, “feebly”, “sweetly and poignantly”, “yearningly”, “rapturously”.

(≒ lusingare, accarezzare)
【General meanings】
① To flatter; to fawn on; to curry favor with.
② To please or delight the senses; to be pleasant, sweet, or beguiling.
【Musical translation examples】
“lusingando”, “flatteringly”, “with sweet flattery”, “smoothly (and pleasingly)”, “obsequiously”, “coaxingly”, “ingratiatingly”, “affably”.
In the dated reflexive use “sich schmeicheln”, the verb can also mean “to flatter oneself”.

The range of possibilities makes this difficult to translate. In the GM sheet, it is rendered as “flatteringly”.

(≒ squillante, fragoroso)
Present participle of “schmettern”.
【General meanings】
① Hurling down or smashing (something).
② Ringing out, blaring, belting out, or sounding piercingly (of sounds or voices).

【Usage notes】
“Brilliantly” is also an expressive musical rendering.

In GM, the Japanese renderings are “響き渡るように” (“resoundingly”) or “高らかに” (“ringingly”); “けたたましく” (“blaringly”) may also be appropriate.

(≒ sorridendo; for an ironic or sardonic smile, sogghignando)

【General meanings】

② (With amusement) Smiling with closed lips.

【Usage notes】
In the RS sheet, examples occur only in Der Rosenkavalier, where the word is translated in sense ①.

(≒ russando)

【General meanings】
① Snoring.
② (Figuratively, of sounds, etc.) Rattling or sounding harshly, like snoring.

In the RS sheet, the only example occurs in Die schweigsame Frau, where the word is translated in sense ①.

【General meanings】
① Rattling, clattering, or buzzing (of machinery, etc.).
② Hoarse; grating (of a voice, etc.).

(≒ rapido; in tempo contexts, presto or allegro)
【General meanings】
Fast; quick; rapid.

(≒ scherzo, burla)
【General meanings】
① (In the idiom ein Schnippchen schlagen) Outwitting someone; getting the better of someone; playing a trick on someone.
② A prank; teasing.
③ (An older use) A snap of the fingers.

The nuance is one of light cunning or a little mischief, rather than sinister betrayal. It is freely translated as “tease”. In the cited stage direction from Das Rheingold, it means snapping one's fingers at the other person as a teasing or contemptuous gesture; it does not specify flicking the person's body.

(≒ sfacciato, impertinente)
【General meanings】
① Pert; impudent; saucy (of one's tone or manner).
② Curt; sharp-tongued.

(≒ già, pure, certamente)
【General meanings】

② (Concessively or emphatically) Admittedly; indeed; certainly, though…
③ (Expressing confidence or reassurance about the future) Surely; in due course.

With a following “aber”, it can also mean “admittedly …, but …”.

(≒ risparmiare, preservare)

③ To spare or exempt (someone from punishment, etc.).

(≒ gridare, urlare)

(≒ speaking tube, speaking trumpet, mouthpiece, spokesman / megafono, portavoce)
【General meanings】

② A spokesperson, publicity representative, or means of communication (for opinions or ideas).
③ A megaphone; a speaking trumpet.

The word is translated as “speaking tube” and, depending on the context, can refer to either:
● a handheld “megaphone” (speaking trumpet) into which one shouts;
● a “speaking tube” aboard a ship or elsewhere (a tube carrying speech from the bridge to the engine room).
The shape and material vary according to the device.

RW gives directions for its use in Der fliegende Holländer, Die Walküre, and Siegfried; RS does so in Die ägyptische Helena. In these works, it is specified as a prop or stage acoustic device, affecting the direction in which the voice is projected or the way it sounds.

★ Historical use (nineteenth to early twentieth century)
These directions can be understood as relating to live acoustic effects in which the direction and resonance of the voice are adjusted by passing it through a tube or speaking trumpet. Details of the device’s material, construction, and installation need to be considered in light of documentation for each work and production.
● In Der fliegende Holländer, the Steuermann is directed to put the Sprachrohr quickly to his mouth and call out over the side of the ship. Elsewhere in the same work, there is also a direction to call out with both hands held to the mouth.
● In Die Walküre, voices from the background, including Helmwige’s, are directed to be heard through a Sprachrohr.
● For Fafner in Siegfried, RW himself gives the direction “durch ein starkes Sprachrohr” (“through a powerful speaking trumpet”). In a later scene, there is also a direction to sing from an opening in the stage floor through a Sprachrohr led to the monster’s mouth from inside. These directions specify the device or route through which the voice passes; specific changes in pitch or timbre need to be considered in light of production documentation and other relevant materials.
● In Die ägyptische Helena, the Muschel (the omniscient shell) has the direction “d. Sprachrohr”.
These can be understood as stage acoustic techniques for making use of vocal projection, a sense of distance, and timbre.

★ Modern use
The following are possible ways of realising these effects in modern performances. Specific examples of their use, the choice of device, and the positioning of singers and equipment depend on the documentation for individual productions.
● Historical reconstruction (acoustic)
Using an actual speaking trumpet or tube to produce live acoustic effects.
● Electronic processing (microphones and loudspeakers)
Reproducing a voice picked up by a microphone through a loudspeaker to create a sense of distance or reverberation.
● A hybrid approach prioritising visual staging
Combining a prop megaphone with electronic processing to achieve both visual staging and acoustic effects.

(≒ tono, suono, nota)

【General meanings】
① A sound, tone colour or tone.
② A tone of voice, manner of speaking or attitude.
③ A musical note or pitch.

GM frequently uses a family of directions centred on Ton, including “Ton!”, “mit Ton!”, “viel Ton!”, “großer Ton!” and “offener Ton”. Depending on the context, these are rendered as “with a rich tone”, “Make the tone resonate”, and so on. For GM, Ton seems to carry musical nuances extending beyond sheer volume. German Ton is inherently polysemous, covering:
● pitch (how high or low a note is), and a unit of interval in expressions such as ein ganzer Ton;
● sound itself as a physical phenomenon;
● tone colour or resonance, close to Klang;
● expression or manner of speaking (Redeweise, Sprechton);
● artistic tone or atmosphere (emotional tone).
In late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century musical usage, Ton often seems to imply “sonority” or “tone quality”; particularly in Schumann, RW, Brahms, Bruckner and GM, it may be interpreted as referring to the “character”, “density” or “spiritual resonance” of a sound.

1. Ton in vocal music
In “Den Ruf der Schildwachen nachahmen offner Ton!” from “Der Schildwache Nachtlied” in Des Knaben Wunderhorn, offener Ton can be understood as asking for more than simply projecting the voice. It can be understood as recreating the situation of a sentry's call sounding through the darkness, or a piercing call of vigilance. It is rendered as “with an open, resonant voice”.

2. grosser Ton in wind playing
The marking “großer Ton!” for the tenor horn at the beginning of the first movement of Symphony No. 7 seems to ask for more than playing f or producing a forceful sound: it suggests the sound's “weight”, “presence” and “texture”. In this sense, grosser Ton probably does not refer to volume alone.

3. Ton! in string playing
GM has numerous passages marked simply “Ton!”, especially conspicuous in legato string passages. Here Ton comes close to calling the performer's attention to the sound. One might infer that what GM wanted to avoid was technically accurate but expressionless playing, or treating a melody merely as a structure.

4. viel Ton

(≒ catalogo di Trenner, numero Trenner)
Abbreviation for Trenner-Verzeichnis.
A number in Franz Trenner’s chronological catalogue of Richard Strauss’s works (Richard Strauss: Werkverzeichnis, 1985; 1993; second revised edition, 1999). TrV and AV are both widely used as reference numbers in research, identification, and the organization of scores.

The difference between TrV and AV
Richard Strauss’s works bear opus numbers assigned during his lifetime (1864–1949), but many early and late works, studies, occasional pieces, and songs have no opus number. Later scholars therefore compiled catalogues to organize and identify the complete body of work systematically. The best-known are AV (Asow numbers) and TrV (Trenner numbers).

Their respective characteristics and functions are as follows.
AV also arranges works chronologically within groups separated by opus-number status and other categories; TrV places compositions in chronological order across those divisions.

1. AV (Asow-Verzeichnis / Müller von Asow numbers)
Compiler: Erich Hermann Müller von Asow
Full title: Richard Strauss: Thematisches Verzeichnis (three volumes, published 1959–1974)
Characteristics and function:
The first large-scale, comprehensive thematic catalogue of Richard Strauss’s works compiled after his death, including musical incipits.
It serves as a scholarly reference and source collection, providing detailed information on opening themes, instrumentation, genesis, autograph locations, first performances and performers, and early printed editions. Müller von Asow died while the third volume was being prepared; Alfons Ott and Franz Trenner completed it. Some later discoveries and information on late works consequently received supplementary treatment.

2. TrV (Trenner-Verzeichnis / Trenner numbers)
Compiler: Franz Trenner
Full title: Richard Strauss: Werkverzeichnis (1985; 1993 edition; second revised edition, 1999, revised by Florian Trenner)
Characteristics and function:
Building on earlier research, this catalogue arranges the works broadly in order of composition, including early works and fragments. Its chronological arrangement surveys Strauss’s output from his early to his late years, making it useful for tracing his creative development and identifying the dates of works. TrV is also used to identify works in Richard Strauss Werke. Kritische Ausgabe and has been adopted as a standard work-number system in library cataloguing.

Examples:
Sonatine No. 1 → TrV 288
Metamorphosen → TrV 290
Oboe Concerto → TrV 292

In summary:
AV: a comprehensive thematic catalogue for investigating incipits, detailed historical and bibliographical information, and the circumstances of composition.
TrV: a chronological catalogue of works, drawing on earlier research to arrange and identify works broadly in chronological order.

These different origins, an earlier detailed thematic catalogue (AV) and a later catalogue that reflects subsequent research and reorganizes the works broadly chronologically (TrV), explain why both sets of numbers are often given in score commentaries and scholarly literature.

(= Werke ohne Opuszahl) Works without an opus number (Op.)

In the catalogue of Ludwig van Beethoven’s works by Georg Kinsky and Hans Halm, published in 1955 as Das Werk Beethovens: Thematisch-bibliographisches Verzeichnis seiner sämtlichen vollendeten Kompositionen, commonly known as the Kinsky–Halm catalogue, works without opus numbers were catalogued separately from those with opus numbers under “WoO (Werke ohne Opuszahl)”, and numbered from WoO 1 to WoO 205. These include early works, short pieces, songs, dances, occasional works and arrangements; the designation does not necessarily mean only unpublished works or works discovered posthumously. A well-known example is the Bagatelle in A minor, Für Elise, WoO 59. Further WoO numbers were added on the basis of new research in the revised catalogue published in 2014.

WoO is an abbreviation of the German “Werke ohne Opuszahl”, meaning “works without an opus number”; it is not a designation unique to Ludwig van Beethoven. It is used in catalogues of several composers to classify works without opus numbers, but the numbering systems are independent for each composer and catalogue.

For Johannes Brahms, WoO numbers are assigned to works without opus numbers, arrangements, cadenzas and similar pieces in Johannes Brahms: Thematisch-Bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, edited by Margit L. McCorkle (1984). For example, the Ungarische Tänze are WoO 1.

For Robert Schumann, WoO numbers were also used in the earlier catalogue by Kurt Hofmann and Siegmar Keil. However, the principal modern scholarly catalogue, Robert Schumann: Thematisch-Bibliographisches Werkverzeichnis, edited by Margit L. McCorkle and commonly known as the Robert-Schumann-Werkverzeichnis (RSW, 2003), assigns WoO 1–8 to works without opus numbers that Schumann published or prepared for publication, while other fragments, unpublished works, projects and similar materials are classified chiefly in the Anhang (appendix).

WoO numbers are also sometimes used for certain works by Felix Mendelssohn Bartholdy in older scores and recording documentation. However, the current standard catalogue, the Mendelssohn-Werkverzeichnis (MWV, 2009), uses its own genre-based numbering system, such as MWV U 136, rather than WoO as its principal formal classification.

Thus, WoO is a classification used for several composers, but it is not a single, unified system of work numbers shared by musicology as a whole. In general contexts, “WoO 59” without a composer’s name often refers to Ludwig van Beethoven’s Für Elise, but in precise writing it is advisable to include the composer’s name.

In musical directions, the function of zu varies considerably depending on the words that follow it.

1. Indicating degree (too / troppo)
Placed before an adjective, it means “too,” with a negative connotation of excess.
“Nicht zu schnell”: not too fast (Non troppo allegro).
“Nicht zu mäßig”: not too moderate or restrained.

2. Specifying the number of players or instruments
“zu 2 (zu zwei)”: with two instruments, or with two players (whether they play in unison depends on the score). (Equivalent to the Italian a 2.)
“zu 3 (zu drei)”: with three instruments.

3. Specifying a state or manner
“zu Ende”: at an end, finished; (in expressions such as “zu Ende spielen”) (playing) through to the end.
“Mund zu”: with the mouth closed (as in humming).

4. Directions for a particular playing technique
“Dämpfer zu”: interpreted here as meaning to put on the mute (sense ③). Incidentally, “Dämpfer auf” in GM also means to put on the mute. See the entry “Dämpfer auf.”

There is no example in this workbook's GM corpus. In Variation II of [RS: Qui], where a flock of sheep is imitated, the term presumably means “flutter-tonguing” (quite apart from the brass, asking the clarinets to do the same at p or pp is diabolically demanding). An early orchestral example of flute flutter-tonguing occurs in Tchaikovsky's The Nutcracker. See also “Zungenstoß.”

(≒ tonguing / colpo di lingua)
【General meanings】
① Thrusting with the tongue.
② (In wind instruments) sound production and articulation through movements of the tongue; tonguing.
【Musical translation examples】
“Tonguing,” “attack.”

In GM, this is translated as “with sharp tonguing.” Some interpret it in the fifth movement of GM’s Symphony No. 2 as “flutter-tonguing.” Since GM explicitly writes “Flatterzunge” elsewhere, I have translated it here as “with sharp tonguing.” However, around bar 402 of the fifth movement, “Zungenstoss” or its abbreviation appears above notes bearing three tremolo strokes, so the precise playing technique still needs to be checked. Still, I think it unlikely that GM, who was also an excellent conductor and thoroughly familiar with the playing techniques of each instrument, would have requested flutter-tonguing from the reed instruments, on which that technique is difficult. I suspect that he was asking for an “extreme” form of tonguing beyond the standard technique; nevertheless, the passage is very loud, and part of me wonders whether there is really any need to work oneself into a frenzy over it.

In GM, it is used mainly where the tempo becomes slower than before, so I have translated it as “slowing down.” I wonder whether simply translating it as “slowly” is slightly inaccurate. If anything, I feel that “ritenuto” may be more appropriate than “rallentando” or “ritardando.” In stage directions in RW and RS, it can also mean “reservedly,” “restraining someone,” or “with restraint.”
However, the sense must follow the context: allmählich zurückhaltend calls for a gradual change, while plötzlich zurückhaltend calls for a sudden one. The word alone should not invariably be equated with ritenuto.
